claims.text: A hybrid approach integrating ab initio molecular dynamics with machine-learning corrections will improve electrical-conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr relative to conventional defect-free analytical models.
The prediction improvement will occur in both the nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The material states considered are nominally pure bulk HfNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% added oxygen.
Ab initio molecular dynamics can model temperature-induced lattice disorder and explicit impurity effects in this alloy.
Machine-learning corrections calibrated against experimental data can correct the conductivity predictions.
The 0–200 K regime captures impurity-dominated scattering effects.
The 300–1200 K regime captures high-temperature phonon scattering and dynamic lattice disorder.
Oxygen impurities and thermally induced lattice disorder disrupt ideal crystal symmetry.
Explicit treatment of oxygen impurities and temperature-induced lattice vibrations accounts for scattering events neglected by perfect-crystal approximations.
Defect scattering is the dominant low-temperature scattering mechanism in the proposed test regime.
Dynamic lattice disorder produces increased phonon scattering at high temperatures.
Accounting for defect and phonon scattering will produce conductivity predictions closer to experiment and reduce error relative to defect-free analytical models.
The improvement will be most pronounced where impurity and phonon scattering are significant.
Conventional analytical predictions assuming defect-free crystals underperform against experiment, especially for oxygen-doped materials and broad temperature ranges.
The approach is applicable to bulk polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr and similar high-entropy alloys.

Its accuracy may diminish for nanostructured materials and outside the stated temperature ranges because of additional phenomena such as very-low-temperature quantum effects or extreme anharmonicity above 1200 K.

contradictions.description: The approach is declared applicable throughout 0–200 K, including nearly zero temperature, but very-low-temperature quantum effects are presented as a reason for diminished accuracy outside that range. The location of this lower applicability limit is therefore internally unclear.

The machine-learning corrections are to be calibrated against experimental data, while the proposed experimental conductivity data are also used for evaluation. No held-out split is specified, so the benchmark may overlap with calibration data and cannot be assumed to be an independent falsification test.
